deep.reconstruction:
Context (from the previous page): Gauss is proving the Lehrsatz (art. 11) that for m indeterminates a,b,c,d,... and every integer n with 0 <= n < m-1, S^n := sum_i a_i^n / prod_{j!=i}(a_i - a_j) = 0. On the previous page he set P = prod_{i<j}(a_i - a_j), the difference product (Vandermonde product). It has m(m-1)/2 factors.

This page:
(1) Define frak{A} = P/((a-b)(a-c)(a-d)...), frak{B} = P/((b-a)(b-c)(b-d)...), frak{C} = P/((c-a)(c-b)(c-d)...), and so on. Each denominator removes m-1 factors of P, up to sign. So each frak{X} is a polynomial (ganze Function) of degree m(m-1)/2 - (m-1) = (m-1)(m-2)/2.
(2) Multiply S^n by P: Q := P*S^n = frak{A} a^n + frak{B} b^n + frak{C} c^n + ... . Q is a polynomial of degree (m-1)(m-2)/2 + n. Since n < m-1, this is less than m(m-1)/2 = deg P.
(3) Divisibility of Q by (a-b), in four steps:
 1°: frak{C}, frak{D}, ... contain the factor (a-b), because their denominators do not involve the pair (a,b).
 2°: Write frak{A} = k (b-c)(b-d)..., where k is the product of the factors of P involving neither a nor b. Then frak{B} = P/((b-a)(b-c)...) = (a-b)(a-c)...(b-c)... k / ((b-a)(b-c)...) = -k (a-c)(a-d)... .
 3°: (b-c)(b-d)... - (a-c)(a-d)... is divisible by a-b. Hence frak{A}+frak{B} = k[(b-c)(b-d)... - (a-c)(a-d)...] is divisible by a-b. Then frak{A} a^n + frak{B} b^n = (frak{A}+frak{B}) a^n - frak{B}(a^n - b^n) is divisible by a-b, because a-b | a^n - b^n.
 4°: Therefore Q is divisible by a-b.
(4) Footnote: the divisibility in 3° is proved like the congruence rule in number theory: if alpha ≡ alpha', beta ≡ beta', ... (mod M), then alpha beta ... ≡ alpha' beta' ... . This is done by telescoping: alpha beta - alpha' beta' = (alpha - alpha') beta + alpha'(beta - beta'), and so on. Here the modulus is the indeterminate a-b, with alpha = b-c, alpha' = a-c, etc.

Continuation (next page): Q is likewise divisible by every factor a_i - a_j. Hence (via substitution/zero arguments) Q is divisible by P. Since deg Q < deg P, Q = 0 and therefore S^n = 0.

[My remark:] Up to sign, Q is the determinant of the matrix with rows (1,...,1), (a,b,...), ..., (a^{m-2},...), (a^n, b^n, ...). For n <= m-2 it has two equal rows, so this is an alternant argument done by hand.
errors: No mathematical errors. The degree count is correct: (m-1)(m-2)/2 + n < m(m-1)/2 iff n < m-1. The sign in frak{B} = -k(a-c)(a-d)... is correct.
Minor point: in 3° the case n=0 is included trivially, since frak{A}+frak{B} itself is divisible.

results.what: sum_i a_i^n / prod_{j!=i}(a_i-a_j) = 0 for 0 <= n <= m-2 (and = 1 for n = m-1, h_{n-m+1} in general), proved by showing P*S^n is divisible by the difference product P and has lower degree
results.modern_name: Euler's partial-fraction identity / divided-difference (Lagrange interpolation) identity; vanishing of alternants with repeated rows
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (18th c.); also Lagrange interpolation (1795); alternant/determinant viewpoint Cauchy (1815)

results.what: Polynomial divisibility of a product difference by a-b, proved via the congruence-multiplication argument (telescoping)
results.modern_name: Congruences modulo a polynomial ideal (a-b); ring homomorphism property
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), for congruences; polynomial congruences also Gauss/Cauchy

deep.surprise_reason: The identity is classical (Euler/Lagrange). Gauss's proof via divisibility by the Vandermonde product and a degree count is a standard, careful elementary argument. The only mildly notable feature is that he explicitly transfers the congruence language of higher arithmetic to divisibility by the indeterminate a-b.
